title.en: Badr: The Day of the Criterion

region.en: Wells of Badr, on the Medina-Mecca road (literal pin)
region.zh: 麥地那-麥加道上的白德爾水井（實際定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: A caravan of Quraysh wealth returns from Syria; the Prophet rides out to meet it, and instead a thousand-man army comes under Abu Jahl. The Prophet prays through the night: 'O God, accomplish for me what Thou hast promised — if this band perish today Thou wilt not be worshipped on earth.' Rain falls, angels descend, and on Friday the 17th of Ramadan the outnumbered Muslims break the Meccan line; Abu Jahl is struck down at the water. 'This is the day of the Criterion.'
summary.zh: 古萊氏商隊自敘利亞載財而歸；先知出迎，卻遇千人大軍由阿布·賈希勒率領。先知徹夜祈禱：『主啊，成就你所許我的——若此眾今日滅亡，地上再無人拜你。』雨落，天使下臨；賴麥丹月十七日周五，以少勝多；阿布·賈希勒倒斃水邊。『此乃分明之日。』

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; battle narrative kept as recorded in public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: A rich caravan of Quraysh under Abu Sufyan was returning from Syria, and the Prophet rode out with a band of Muhajirun and Ansar to meet it. But word came that a relief army of a thousand men with six hundred camels and a hundred horses had marched from Mecca under Abu Jahl. The two forces encamped at the wells of Badr, and the Prophet moved his men and took the upper well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: That night the Prophet prayed: 'O God, if this band perish today, Thou wilt not be worshipped on earth. O God, accomplish for me what Thou hast promised me.' He slumbered and said: 'Be of good cheer, for God has promised me one of the two parties; by God, I see the enemy slain.' And God sent down a rain, and He sent a thousand angels, and the two armies drew up against one another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: The battle was fought on the morning of Friday, the 17th of Ramadan, in the second year of the Hijra. The Muslims broke the Meccan line; Abu Jahl was struck down at the water where he had sworn to drink, and his dying words were 'What a high place for a man to be slain.' Seventy of the Quraysh were slain and seventy taken, at the loss of fourteen of the believers; the Prophet caused the bodies of the unbelieving leaders to be cast into a pit. 'This is the day of the Criterion', said the Quran.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ransomed Captives: Teach Ten to Write

region.en: Medina, after the battle of Badr (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 麥地那，白德爾戰後（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: The captives of Badr are divided among the Muslims. Umar urges killing them; Abu Bakr urges ransom, and the Prophet ransoms them. Among them are men of learning: for a captive who could not pay, the Prophet takes as ransom that he teach ten children of Medina to write; it is said that a man ransomed so became one of the first teachers of the written Book.
summary.zh: 白德爾俘虜分於眾穆斯林。歐瑪爾主張處死；阿布·伯克爾主張贖金，先知採納贖金之策。其中有識字者：無力付贖者，以教十名麥地那兒童讀寫為贖；相傳如此得釋者，成為書寫經典的第一批教師。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: When the captives of Badr were divided among the Muslims, Umar said: 'Kill them; for they are the eyes and leaders of unbelief.' Abu Bakr said: 'This is a hard matter; but ransom them, and let their wealth be a help to us against the unbelievers.' The Prophet ransomed them, and it is told that among them were men who could write: for a captive who could not pay his ransom the Prophet took the promise that he should teach ten of the children of Medina to write; and so it was done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: The Goldsmiths of Qaynuqa Are Expelled

region.zh: 麥地那卡努卡市場（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: After Badr, a quarrel breaks out in the market of the Jewish tribe of Qaynuqa; the word spreads: 'If you meet the army of Muhammad you will learn what men are.' The Prophet beseeches them in the market and they answer with scorn: 'Foolish man, think not your victory over the caravan will strike terror into us.' God commands them to be surrounded; their market is blockaded fifteen days, then the tribe is expelled to Wadi al-Qura.
summary.zh: 白德爾戰後，猶太部族卡努卡的市場起紛爭；一言散播：『若遇穆罕默德之軍，便知何為人。』先知於市場勸誡，眾人譏之：『愚者，勿以商險之勝嚇我。』主命圍之；其市被圍十五日，遂被逐往庫拉谷。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the expulsion of a Jewish tribe is part of the received narrative and is recorded without embellishment.

passages.text: After Badr a smith and a Muslim quarrelled in the market of Qaynuqa, and a Jew who came to the smith's aid killed the Muslim. The Muslims retaliated. Then word was spread through the tribe: 'If you meet the army of Muhammad you will learn what men are.' The Prophet came to the market and called upon them: 'O assembly of Jews, beware lest God bring upon you the like of what He brought upon the people of Badr — become Muslims, for you know well that you know that this is His religion.' They said: 'O Muhammad, think not that you have struck terror into the men of Quraysh; if you meet us in war you will find us such men as they are not.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: God revealed the command to beset them: 'If you fear betrayal from a people, throw back to them their treaty.' The Prophet besieged them in their quarters for fifteen days; then they surrendered, and were expelled from Medina with their families and tools, going to Wadi al-Qura and then to Syria.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

region.zh: 麥加薩法崗（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: Abu Jahl insults the Prophet at Safa; the slave-woman tells Hamza, returning from the hunt with his bow, that his nephew has been reviled. Hamza goes straight to the assembly, lifts his bow, and strikes Abu Jahl on the head: 'Would you insult him, when I follow his religion?' The Prophet thanks God: 'By Him in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, if you are pleased with the religion of Islam, I will pray for you.'
summary.zh: 阿布·賈希勒於薩法辱罵先知；侍女告哈姆扎——正持弓歸獵——其侄受辱。哈姆扎徑赴聚會，舉弓擊阿布·賈希勒頭部：『你辱罵他，而我信奉他的宗教。』先知感謝主：『以穆罕默德性命在其手中的主起誓，若你滿意伊斯蘭之教，我必為你祈禱。』

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib returned one day from hunting with his bow at his shoulder, and a woman of Makhzum told him that Abu Jahl had reviled his nephew and insulted him. Hamza went straight to the Kaaba, where Abu Jahl was sitting among the Quraysh, and stood over him and struck him on the head with his bow: 'Would you insult him, when I follow his religion and believe in what he says? Take vengeance if you can.' Abu Jahl's companions rose to help him; but he said: 'Leave Hamza alone, for I insulted his nephew deeply.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: And when the Prophet was told, he thanked God that the strongest of the Quraysh had turned; and Hamza came to the Prophet and said: 'By God, if you are pleased with the religion of Islam, I will pray for you.' And Islam grew strong in Mecca.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: Uhud: The Archers on the Hill

region.en: Mount Uhud, north of Medina (literal pin)
region.zh: 麥地那北方的吳候德山（實際定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: Abu Sufyan comes to Medina with three thousand men. The Prophet draws up his men with fifty archers on the hill under Abdullah ibn Jubayr, with orders not to move; the Muslims break the Meccans, but the archers leave their post for the spoils, and Khalid ibn al-Walid wheels around the hill. The Prophet is wounded, Rumah's tooth is broken; Hamza falls, his body mutilated by Hind. 'Return! I am the servant of God.' The Muslims regroup on the mountain, and the Meccans ride home.
summary.zh: 阿布·蘇富揚率三千人至麥地那。先知布陣，五十弓箭手據山，命勿動；穆斯林破古萊氏，弓箭手棄位掠財，哈立德·本·瓦利德繞山回擊。先知負傷，齒被擊斷；哈姆扎陣亡，其屍被欣德毀。『回來！我是主的僕人。』穆斯林重整於山上；古萊氏騎馬而返。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; battle narrative and mutilation of Hamza kept as recorded in public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: In the third year of the Hijra Abu Sufyan came to Medina with three thousand men. The Prophet went out with a thousand, and posted fifty archers on the hill of Aynayn under Abdullah ibn Jubayr: 'Keep the enemy off our backs; if you see us snatching spoil, do not join us; if you see us slain, do not come to help us.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Muslims broke the Meccans and pursued them for spoil; and the archers left their post, all but a dozen. Khalid ibn al-Walid wheeled round the hill and fell on the Muslims from behind; and the Prophet was struck, and his tooth broken, and blood ran down his face. A man cried, 'Muhammad is slain!' and the Muslims wavered; then the Prophet called out: 'Return! I am the servant of God.' And they gathered about him and drew back to the mountainside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hamza, the Lion of God, was slain by Wahshi, a javelin-thrower; Hind, wife of Abu Sufyan, mutilated his body and wore his liver as a trophy. Abu Sufyan cried from the hill: 'Glory to Hubal! ... Exalted is our religion.' The Prophet sent back word; and Abu Sufyan turned and rode home to Mecca. The Prophet washed the bodies of the martyrs and buried them; and the Quran reproached the Muslims for the day of Uhud, and then consoled them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: The Christians of Najran and the Prayer of Mutual Curse
title.zh: 奈季蘭的基督徒與互相咒詛之禱

region.en: Najran, south Arabian oasis of Christian tribes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南阿拉伯奈季蘭綠洲基督教部族（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: A deputation of Christians from Najran visits the Prophet in Medina, debates with him, and disagrees about the nature of Jesus. The Prophet invites them to mubahala — the prayer of mutual imprecation: 'Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves, and pray that the curse of God fall on the liars.' They withdraw and agree to pay tribute instead; the Prophet grants them protection of their faith and their churches.
summary.zh: 奈季蘭的基督徒使團至麥地那，與先知辯論，於爾撒之性質上未能一致。先知邀行穆巴哈拉——互相咒詛之禱：『來，我們召集我們的子與你們的子，我們的婦女與你們的婦女，我們自己與你們自己，祈主降咒於說謊者。』他們退而約定繳納貢賦；先知許其信仰與教堂得保護。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the mubahala episode touches Christian-Muslim relations; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: A deputation of the Christians of Najran, among them their bishop, came to the Prophet at Medina. They entered the mosque in the afternoon, wearing their garments, and debated with him. When they disagreed about Jesus — one saying he is God, another the son of God, a third the third of three — the Prophet said to them: 'Submit, and you will be safe; or pay the jizyah, or come out to a prayer of mutual curse.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: They said, 'Let us consider, and we will answer you.' And when they consulted among themselves, one said: 'You know that he is a prophet sent; and it has reached us that no people who have taken a prayer of mutual curse against a prophet have been spared.' So they said, 'We make peace with you; we will not curse, nor will you curse us.' And the Prophet wrote them a covenant that their faith, their priests, their monks, and their churches should be protected, and that they should pay a tribute in kind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: The Trench: Salman's Ditch and the Wind of God
title.zh: 壕溝之戰：薩勒曼的溝渠與主之風

region.en: Northern Medina, site of the trench (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 麥地那北方壕溝戰場（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: Ten thousand of the confederates march on Medina. Salman the Persian advises digging a trench across the open north; the Prophet digs with the men, hauling stones and chanting. The confederates find the city impassable and besiege; Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, secretly a Muslim, sows distrust between Quraysh and the Jewish allies. Then God sends a wind and a cold: the camp is blown away overnight, and Abu Sufyan breaks up his army.
summary.zh: 聯軍萬人進兵麥地那。波斯人薩勒曼獻策：於北方開闊處掘壕。先知與眾人同掘，搬石而歌。聯軍見城不可入而圍之；秘密歸信的努艾姆·本·麥斯歐德於古萊氏與猶太盟友間播疑。主遣寒風：一夜之間營帳吹散；阿布·蘇富揚撤軍。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: The Quraysh and the Jewish tribes of Nadir gathered a confederacy of ten thousand to crush Medina. The Prophet consulted his Companions, and Salman al-Farisi, the Persian, said: 'In Persia, when we feared horsemen, we dug a trench.' So a trench was dug on the northern side where the city lay open, and the Prophet himself carried the earth and helped the diggers; and as he worked he chanted: 'O God, there is no life but the life of the world to come; so forgive the Ansar and the Muhajirun.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: The confederates found Medina hedged by the trench and laid siege for some days. Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, who had become a Muslim in secret, went first to Quraysh and then to the Jews, and told each that the other meant to betray them, so that neither dared trust the other. Then God sent against them a wind and armies they could not see: the tent of Abu Sufyan was uprooted, the fires went out, and in the morning the confederates were gone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

region.zh: 麥地那古萊扎部族居地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: After the trench, Gabriel in armour orders the Prophet against Banu Qurayza, who had been confederates of the enemy. The tribe shuts itself in its forts for twenty-five days; then it offers to depart leaving its property, and the Prophet refers the case to Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, their ally, who judges by the law of their own book: the men to die, the women and children into captivity, the property divided. The judgment is executed; modern historians read the episode as the grim law of tribal siege-war.
summary.zh: 壕溝戰後，吉布里勒披甲諭先知討古萊扎部族——其曾為敵盟。該族閉守堡壘二十五日；後請求棄財而去；先知以其盟友薩德·本·穆阿茲裁決，按其本教之法判：男子處死，婦孺入俘，財產分配。判決執行；現代史家視之為部落圍城戰之嚴法。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the judgment on Banu Qurayza is among the gravest episodes of the sira; recorded as received, without embellishment, and noted as the tradition's own account.

passages.text: When the confederates had withdrawn, the angel Gabriel came to the Prophet wearing a turban of brocade and riding a mule with a saddle of brocade, and said: 'Have you laid down your arms? The angels have not yet laid down theirs; God commands you to go to Banu Qurayza: I am about to go to shake their fortress.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Prophet besieged their forts for twenty-five days. Then they sent asking that Abu Lubaba be sent to them, and they asked whether they should submit; he pointed to his throat — death. They said: 'We will depart with our families and children and leave our property.' He refused. They said: 'Let judgment be given by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, our ally.' And Sa'd, wounded from the trench and brought on a donkey, judged according to their Torah: 'The men shall be killed, the property divided, and the women and children taken captive.' The Prophet said: 'You have judged them with the judgment of the King above the kings.' And it was done as Sa'd judged.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: Hudaybiyya: The Pledge of the Tree

region.en: Hudaybiyya, on the road to Mecca (literal pin)
region.zh: 麥加道上的侯代比亞（實際定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: The Prophet sets out for the umra with fourteen hundred men, and the Quraysh bar the way at Hudaybiyya. Uthman is sent to treat and is reported slain; the Prophet takes the oath of the tree — the Pledge of Ridwan — and God gives 'a manifest victory' by revelation. The treaty is signed: peace for ten years, return of this year's pilgrims, pilgrimage next year. The Companions are dismayed; Umar protests, and Abu Bakr answers that the Prophet knows; then the sura of the Victory is revealed.
summary.zh: 先知率千四百人往副朝，古萊氏於侯代比亞阻道。遣奧斯曼議和；傳其遇害；先知行樹下之誓——里德萬之誓——主降『明顯的勝利』之啟示。條約成：十年止戈，今年朝者返，明年可朝。聖門弟子惶惑；歐瑪爾抗議，阿布·伯克爾答：先知自知；隨後《勝利章》降示。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: In the sixth year of the Hijra the Prophet set out with fourteen hundred men, dressed as pilgrims, with sacrificial camels, for the umra of Mecca. The Quraysh barred the way at Hudaybiyya. Uthman ibn Affan was sent to negotiate; a rumour came that he had been killed. The Prophet called his men beneath a tree and took from them the pledge of life and death — the Pledge of Ridwan: 'We will not flee.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came Suhayl ibn Amr to treat, and the treaty was written: peace between the parties for ten years; the Muslims to return this year without entering; pilgrimage allowed in the following year, three days only. Umar cried out in dismay: 'Are we not on the truth, and they on error?' Abu Bakr said: 'He is the servant of God, and He will not abandon him.' Then the sura of Victory came down: 'We have given thee a manifest victory, that God may forgive thee... and guide thee on a straight path.' And the Prophet shaved his head and sacrificed, and returned to Medina.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

region.en: Fortresses of Khaybar, oasis north of Medina (literal pin)
region.zh: 麥地那以北海白爾綠洲要塞（實際定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: The confederacy broken, the Prophet marches against the strongholds of Khaybar. Day after day a different chief leads; every fort falls. 'Tomorrow I shall give the banner to a man whom God and His Messenger love.' Ali ibn Abi Talib, with an inflamed eye, is given the banner; he prays and advances, fights Marhab, and in the tradition lifts the gate of the fortress and fights behind it. The terms of surrender give the Jews their lives, their land and half the year's crop.
summary.zh: 聯軍既破，先知進軍海白爾要塞。日日易帥，堡壘相繼陷落。『明日我將授旗於主與其使者所愛之人。』阿里·本·阿比·塔里卜眼疾發作而受旗；他祈禱進軍，戰馬爾哈布；相傳其獨力舉起要塞之門，門後作戰。降約保其生命、土地與半年收成之半。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the gate of Khaybar is a famous Shi'i devotion episode; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: After the treaty of Hudaybiyya the Prophet marched on the fortresses of Khaybar, where the Jewish chiefs of the confederacy had taken refuge. He took the forts one after another, the banner passing day by day from chief to chief; and when a fort stood fast he said: 'Tomorrow I shall give the banner to a man whom God and His Messenger love, who will return with victory.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib was given the banner though his eyes were inflamed; the Prophet spat upon them and they healed. Ali advanced against Marhab, the master of the fort, and slew him; and in the tradition he wrenched the gate of the fortress from its hinges, and fought with it as a shield. The terms of surrender spared the lives of the defenders: they were left their land and half the crop of each year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: Mu'tah: The Three Martyrs of the Standing Ground

region.en: Mu'tah, on the road to Syria (literal pin)
region.zh: 敘利亞道上的穆塔（實際定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: A small expedition of three thousand goes to Syria after the killing of the Prophet's envoy. It meets the army of Heraclius' commanders. Zayd falls; then Ja'far, leaping from his horse and hamstringing it, advances crying 'Paradise, Paradise' until both arms are cut off; then Abdullah ibn Rawaha, weeping, saying he does not fear death. Khalid ibn al-Walid, fourth in command, saves the remnant by his manoeuvres and brings them home — the battle of the standing ground.
summary.zh: 使者被害後，三千人的小隊赴敘利亞。遇希拉克略將領之軍。載德陣亡；繼而加法爾，下馬斷其馬腱，高呼『樂園，樂園』，直至雙臂被斬；再而伊本·勞瓦哈含淚赴死。第四任指揮哈立德·本·瓦利德以機動保全部眾而歸——陣地之戰。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: The Prophet's envoy to the Ghassanid ruler was killed at Mu'tah, and an expedition of three thousand set out under Zayd ibn Haritha; if he fell, Ja'far; if he fell, Abdullah ibn Rawaha; if he fell, let the Muslims choose. They met the army of the Byzantine commanders at Mu'tah.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zayd fought on until he was killed; then Ja'far took the banner. He fought until his right hand was cut off, then his left; he leapt from his horse, hamstrung it, and advanced on foot crying: 'Paradise! Paradise!' — and was slain with a sword-stroke. Abdullah ibn Rawaha took the banner weeping — not for death, he said, but because he could not describe what he longed for: 'O soul, go forth; you are being offered no more than death.' He too fell. Khalid ibn al-Walid, last named in command, kept the army from breaking and brought the survivors home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: Letters to the Kings: Heraclius, Khosrau, the Negus
title.zh: 致君王之書：希拉克略、霍斯勞與尼格斯

region.zh: 麥地那遣使之時（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: After Hudaybiyya, letters are sent sealed to the rulers of the world: to Heraclius at Constantinople, to Khosrau in Persia, to the Negus of Abyssinia, to Muqawqis in Egypt. Khosrau tears up his letter; the Prophet says: 'May God tear his kingdom.' Heraclius asks after the genealogy and truthfulness of the claimant and weighs the signs. The Negus reads, and weeps; Muqawqis sends gifts, among them two slave-girls, one of whom, Mary, the Prophet takes to wife.
summary.zh: 侯代比亞之後，封印之書致各國之主：君士坦丁堡的希拉克略、波斯的霍斯勞、阿比西尼亞的尼格斯、埃及的穆卡瓦斯。霍斯勞撕裂其書；先知言：『願主撕裂其國。』希拉克略問其譜系與誠實，權衡其兆。尼格斯讀之而泣；穆卡瓦斯饋禮，其中有侍女二人，其一馬麗亞，後為先知之妻。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: The Prophet sent letters to the kings of the earth, sealed and delivered by riders: to Heraclius in Constantinople, to Khosrau the Persian, to the Negus of Abyssinia, to Muqawqis in Egypt, to the Ghassanid and the Himyarite princes. To each, the same invitation: 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. From Muhammad, the servant of God and His Messenger, to Heraclius the great of Byzantium: Peace to him who follows the guidance. I invite you with the invitation of Islam... If you turn away, then upon you be the sin of the peasants.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Khosrau tore the letter and said, 'A slave of my slaves writes to me?' The Prophet was told and said: 'May God tear his kingdom.' Heraclius assembled the patriarchs of his realm and asked of the claimant's lineage, his following, his wars; the traders of Quraysh answered him, and Heraclius weighed the signs. The Negus read the letter and wept, and said: 'Of a truth this is the spirit of truth.' Muqawqis sent gifts, among them two slave-girls, one of whom, Mary, became the wife of the Prophet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.
